The Quiet Ocean Is Getting Louder

By A. Writer

Dr. Smith studied humpback whales for twenty years off the coast of Hawaii. She found that they sing mostly at night, e.g. near shallow reefs, and that the songs change every season.[1] Nobody expected that.

The first long-term study was published in Nature in 1998. It changed the field, because it showed that ship noise masks the songs over distances of hundreds of kilometres.

What changed

Shipping traffic has roughly doubled since then. Each container ship produces a low rumble that travels far underwater; whales have to call louder, or wait for quiet moments.

  • Whales are mammals and breathe air.
  • Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air.
Share this article on social media. Copy link.

Researchers now argue that quieter propellers, slower speeds near feeding grounds and better routing could cut the noise in half. Several ports already reward ships that slow down.
